tool.name: SSH
tool.tagline: Secure remote shells, file transfer and tunnels with OpenSSH
tool.description: SSH (Secure Shell) gives you an encrypted, authenticated connection to another machine for running commands, copying files and tunnelling network traffic. OpenSSH is the implementation on virtually every Linux server, Mac and modern Windows, and it is how developers reach servers, Git hosts and cloud VMs.

glossary.def: The SSH server program. It runs on the remote machine, waits for connections (normally on port 22) and logs people in.
The free SSH software almost everyone uses: the ssh, scp, sftp and ssh-keygen commands plus the sshd server, included in Linux, macOS and Windows.
In SSH, one login or command running over a connection, from connecting until you exit.
In SSH, keys your local ssh program catches itself instead of sending them on: Enter then ~ then . ends a frozen connection.
A server's own key pair, made when SSH is installed. The server proves it holds the private half, so you know you reached the right machine.
The file ~/.ssh/known_hosts where ssh remembers each server's host key, so it can warn you if a server suddenly shows a different one.
A short code worked out from a key, like SHA256:Xr3...9kQ. Two keys with the same fingerprint are the same key, so comparing fingerprints is an easy check.
An attacker who secretly sits between you and the machine you want, pretending to each side to be the other so they can read or change the traffic.
A password that locks a private key file, so the key is useless to anyone who copies the file without knowing it.
The modern, recommended type of SSH key: short, fast and secure.
The file ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on a server listing the public keys allowed to log in to that account, one per line.
A small background program that holds your unlocked private keys in memory, so you type each passphrase only once.
A special file that programs on the same machine use to talk to each other, the way a network connection links programs on different machines.
Letting a server you log in to use the ssh-agent on your own computer (ssh -A), so you can log in onward from there. Risky: that server's admins can use your keys too.
Carrying network connections for another program through an SSH connection, so a service on one side can be reached from the other side.
A single, carefully secured server that people log in to first in order to reach private machines behind it that accept SSH only from there.
The ssh setting (or -J option) that reaches a machine through a bastion, keeping the connection encrypted end to end and your keys on your own computer.
A simple relay that apps can ask to connect them to any address; with ssh -D the connections leave from the SSH server, as if you were there.
A small extra settings file in a name.d/ folder, read along with the main configuration file, so you can add settings without editing the main file.
Carrying many separate sessions over one connection at the same time, so later ones skip the slow connection setup.
In SSH, one separate stream of traffic inside a connection: a shell, a command, a file transfer or a forwarded port.
The ssh setting that turns on connection reuse: the first connection to a host becomes the master and later ones ride on it.
A public key plus details (owner, allowed logins, expiry) signed by a trusted key, so servers can trust it without listing each key.
In an SSH certificate, a login name (or host name) the certificate is valid for.
The step at the start of an SSH connection where both sides arrive at the same secret encryption keys without ever sending them over the network.
The SSH copy command: copies files to or from another machine, like cp with host:path for the remote side.
A program that copies or syncs files and folders, sending only what changed; usually used over SSH.

concepts.name: Connecting with ssh
concepts.summary: `ssh user@host` opens a shell on a remote machine over an encrypted connection; -p picks the port, and exit or Ctrl-d closes it.
concepts.why: Reaching servers and cloud machines over SSH is a basic skill for anyone who builds or runs software.
concepts.body:
Servers usually sit in a data centre or the cloud, far from any keyboard. To work on one, you type commands on your own computer and have them run over there. **SSH** (Secure Shell) does exactly that: it gives you a shell on a **remote** machine, one somewhere else on the network. A machine you connect to is called a **host**.

SSH is a **protocol**: an agreed set of rules two programs follow to talk over a network, like two people agreeing on a language. The **client**, `ssh`, runs on your computer and starts the connection. The server program, **sshd**, runs on the remote machine and waits for connections.

A machine can run many network programs at once, so each one waits on a numbered **port**, like flats in one building; sshd normally uses port 22. The machine itself is found by its name (`server.example.com`) or its numeric **IP address** (`203.0.113.10`).

Everything sent over SSH is scrambled so only the two ends can read it: that's **encryption**. Both sides also prove who they are, which is called **authentication**. The server shows its host key, a key that proves it's the right machine (next lesson), and you give a password or, better, a key.

The basic command:

- `ssh alice@server.example.com` logs in as user `alice`. Without `alice@`, your own username is used.
- `-p 2222` connects to a different port.
- `-i ~/.ssh/work_key` picks which key file to use.
- `-v` (up to `-vvv`) prints details when a connection fails.

Once connected you get a normal shell on the remote machine, and whatever you type runs there. That stretch from login to logout is your **session**; `exit` or `Ctrl-d` ends it.

If the connection freezes (say, your laptop switched Wi-Fi), the remote side can't hear you, so Ctrl-C does nothing. Use an **escape sequence**, keys your local `ssh` catches itself: Enter, then `~`, then `.` kills the session. `~?` lists the others.

On the very first connection to a host, ssh shows a short code identifying the server's key (its fingerprint) and asks whether to trust it. The next lesson explains why that matters.

**OpenSSH**, the usual SSH software, ships with Linux, macOS and Windows 10/11, so `ssh` is normally already installed. A machine that accepts connections needs the server package too (`openssh-server` on Debian/Ubuntu).
concepts.code:
ssh alice@203.0.113.10             # log in as alice
ssh -p 2222 deploy@build.example.com
ssh -i ~/.ssh/work_ed25519 alice@server
ssh -v alice@server                # show details of a failing connection
# inside the session
whoami && hostname                 # alice / server
exit                               # or Ctrl-d
# frozen session? press:  Enter  ~  .
takeaways: `ssh user@host`; -p for the port, -i for a key, -v for details
exit or Ctrl-d closes; Enter ~ . kills a frozen session
Both sides prove who they are: the server with its host key, you with a password or key
pitfalls: Pressing Ctrl-C on a frozen session; it is sent to the remote side, use Enter ~ . instead.

quiz.q: A session froze after your laptop changed networks. How do you end it from your side?
quiz.explain: The ~. escape sequence is handled by your local ssh program, so it works even when the remote side can't be reached.

concepts.name: Host keys and known_hosts
concepts.summary: The server's host key is recorded in ~/.ssh/known_hosts on first connect; a changed key triggers a loud warning.
concepts.why: Host key checking is what stops an attacker sitting between you and the server from pretending to be your server.
concepts.body:
Each SSH server has its own key pair, the **host key**, created when SSH is installed (`/etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key` and friends). When you connect, the server proves it holds the private half. That stops a **man-in-the-middle**: an attacker who sits between you and the server and pretends to be it.

A key is long, so people compare its **fingerprint** instead: a short code worked out from the key, like `SHA256:Xr3...9kQ`. Same key, same fingerprint.

The first time, your client has nothing to compare with, so it asks:

`The authenticity of host 'server (203.0.113.10)' can't be established. ED25519 key fingerprint is SHA256:...`

Typing `yes` stores the key in `~/.ssh/known_hosts`. Ideally you check the fingerprint first, comparing it with the output of `ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub` run on the server (or with what your cloud provider's web page shows).

On later connections, ssh checks the key against known_hosts. If it differs you get `WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED!` and the connection is refused. Either the server was reinstalled, or someone is attacking. Only after confirming the server really was rebuilt, remove the old entry with `ssh-keygen -R hostname` and connect again.

A useful setting for scripts: `StrictHostKeyChecking accept-new` automatically accepts keys for **new** hosts but still refuses **changed** ones. Never use `StrictHostKeyChecking no` with `UserKnownHostsFile /dev/null` outside throwaway test machines; it switches the protection off entirely.
concepts.code:
# on the server: show its host key fingerprint
ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub
# 256 SHA256:Xr3...9kQ root@server (ED25519)

# on the client
ssh-keygen -F server.example.com     # is it in known_hosts?
ssh-keygen -R server.example.com     # forget a (legitimately) changed key
ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new ci@server.example.com
takeaways: known_hosts pins each server's host key
Verify the fingerprint on first connect when it matters
accept-new trusts new hosts but still rejects changed keys
pitfalls: Reflexively deleting the known_hosts entry on a host-key warning without checking why the key changed.

quiz.q: What does `StrictHostKeyChecking accept-new` do when a known host presents a different key?
quiz.explain: accept-new only auto-accepts unknown hosts; a changed key for a known host is still an error.

concepts.name: Generating SSH key pairs
concepts.summary: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 creates a private key you keep secret and a .pub public key you hand out.
concepts.why: Key-based login is more secure and more convenient than passwords, and it is required by Git hosts and most clouds.
concepts.body:
Logging in with a key uses a **key pair**: a **private key** that never leaves your machine, and a **public key** you can give to any server. To let you in, the server sends a random challenge that only the matching private key can answer (it "signs" it). The private key itself never travels.

Create one with `ssh-keygen`:

- `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "alice@laptop"` makes `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` (private) and `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub` (public). The `-C` comment helps you recognise the key later.
- **Ed25519** is the modern key type: small, fast and secure. Use `-t rsa -b 4096` only for old systems that don't support it.

Set a **passphrase** when asked: a password that locks the private key file itself, so a stolen laptop or backup copy doesn't hand out access. The ssh-agent lesson removes the cost of typing it.

The public key is one line like `ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3Nz... alice@laptop`; it's safe to paste into GitHub, a cloud provider's settings page or a colleague's server.

The private key file must be readable only by you (`chmod 600`); ssh refuses to use a key that others could read. Hardware keys (`-t ed25519-sk`) keep the private key on a small USB security key, such as a YubiKey, and need a touch of it to use.

Make one key per device rather than copying one key everywhere. If a laptop is lost, you remove just its public key from your servers.
concepts.code:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "alice@laptop"
# Enter file in which to save the key (~/.ssh/id_ed25519): <Enter>
# Enter passphrase: ********
ls -l ~/.ssh
# -rw------- 1 alice alice  464 id_ed25519        <- private, keep secret
# -rw-r--r-- 1 alice alice  101 id_ed25519.pub    <- public, share freely
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
# ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAI... alice@laptop
ssh-keygen -lf ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub     # show its fingerprint
takeaways: The private key stays on your machine; the .pub file is safe to share
Prefer ed25519; lock the private key with a passphrase
One key per device makes cutting off a lost device simple
pitfalls: Pasting the private key (no .pub) into a website or chat; if that happens, generate a new key.

quiz.q: Which file do you paste into GitHub's 'SSH keys' settings?
quiz.explain: Only the public key (.pub) is shared; the private key never leaves your machine.

concepts.name: authorized_keys and ssh-copy-id
concepts.summary: A server trusts your public key once it is listed in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys of the target account, with strict permissions.
concepts.why: This is how key-based login is actually switched on for an account, and permission mistakes here are the top cause of failures.
concepts.body:
On the server, each account lists the public keys allowed to log in as it in **authorized_keys** (`~/.ssh/authorized_keys`), one key per line.

The easy way to add yours is `ssh-copy-id`, which logs in (with your password, the last time you will need it) and appends the key:

`ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub alice@server`

Doing it by hand works too: append the contents of the `.pub` file to `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` on the server.

**Permissions** matter because sshd (with the default `StrictModes yes`) ignores the file if others could have tampered with it:

- `~/.ssh` must be `700`, `authorized_keys` should be `600`, and the home directory must not be writable by other users.
- The files must be owned by the account.

When key login fails and falls back to asking for a password, run `ssh -v` on the client (look for "Offering public key" and the server's reply) and check the server log (`journalctl -u ssh` or `/var/log/auth.log`), which says exactly why a key was refused.

Each line can carry **options** before the key to limit it: `from="10.0.0.0/8"` accepts the key only from that range of IP addresses, and `command="/usr/local/bin/backup",restrict` makes a key that may only run one backup script.
concepts.code:
ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub alice@server   # asks for the password once
ssh alice@server                                     # now logs in with the key

# manual alternative, on the server:
mkdir -p ~/.ssh && chmod 700 ~/.ssh
echo 'ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3Nz... alice@laptop' >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys

# a restricted key: may only run the backup script, only from one network
# from="10.0.0.0/8",command="/usr/local/bin/backup",restrict ssh-ed25519 AAAA... backup
takeaways: ~/.ssh/authorized_keys lists keys allowed for that account
ssh-copy-id installs your key; ~/.ssh 700, authorized_keys 600
Server logs explain refused keys; ssh -v shows what was offered
pitfalls: A group-writable home or .ssh directory: sshd silently ignores the keys and asks for a password.

quiz.q: Key login keeps falling back to a password prompt. Which is a likely cause?
options: The public key is in known_hosts
The private key has a passphrase
quiz.explain: With StrictModes, sshd ignores authorized_keys when the directory or file permissions are too open.

concepts.name: Running remote commands and piping data
concepts.summary: ssh host 'command' runs one command remotely and returns its output and exit status, and standard input and output flow through the connection.
concepts.why: One-off remote commands and pipes over SSH are the backbone of scripts, backups and quick checks.
concepts.body:
Give ssh a command after the host and it runs that command instead of an interactive shell, then exits with the **command's exit status**:

`ssh web1 'df -h /'` prints the disk usage and returns.

Quoting matters. The command string is sent to the remote shell, so quote it to stop your **local** shell from expanding things: `ssh web1 'echo $HOME'` prints the remote home, while `ssh web1 "echo $HOME"` prints your local one.

Standard input and output travel through the connection, so ssh works inside a pipe:

- `ssh db 'pg_dump shop' > shop.sql` saves a copy of a remote PostgreSQL database into a file on your machine.
- `tar czf - project | ssh backup 'cat > project.tgz'` sends a bundle of files (a tar archive) the other way.
- `ssh web1 'journalctl -u nginx -n 100' | grep 500` filters remote logs locally.

When you pass a command, ssh doesn't set up a terminal on the remote side, which is right for pipes. Interactive programs (`top`, `sudo` asking for a password, `vim`, `tmux`) need one: add `-t`.

Exit status propagates, so scripts can use it: `ssh web1 'systemctl is-active nginx' || alert`. For running the same command on many hosts, a simple loop works; tools like Ansible are built on exactly this.
concepts.code:
ssh web1 'uptime'                         # runs remotely, prints, exits
ssh web1 'echo $HOME'                     # /home/alice  (remote)
ssh web1 "echo $HOME"                     # expanded locally first!
ssh -t web1 'sudo systemctl restart nginx'   # needs a terminal for sudo's password prompt
ssh db 'pg_dump shop | gzip' > shop.sql.gz   # stream remote -> local
tar czf - src | ssh backup 'cat > src.tgz'   # stream local -> remote
for h in web1 web2; do ssh "$h" 'hostname; uptime'; done
ssh web1 'test -f /etc/maintenance' && echo "in maintenance"
takeaways: ssh host 'cmd' returns the command's output and exit status
Single-quote the command so the remote shell expands it
Add -t for interactive programs; leave it off for pipes
pitfalls: Using double quotes, so your own shell fills in $VARIABLES before the remote one sees them.

quiz.q: Why does `ssh host "echo $USER"` print your local username?
options: The remote USER is not set
The local shell expands $USER inside double quotes before ssh runs
quiz.explain: Double quotes allow local expansion; single quotes pass $USER to the remote shell.

quiz.q: Which flag do you need for `ssh host 'htop'` to work?
quiz.explain: htop is interactive and needs a terminal, which -t asks ssh to set up.

concepts.name: ssh-agent: unlock once, use all day
concepts.summary: ssh-agent keeps your unlocked keys in memory, so you type a passphrase once per login instead of on every connection.
concepts.why: Passphrase-protected keys are only practical with an agent, and Git over SSH depends on it.
concepts.body:
A passphrase-protected private key must be unlocked before each use. **ssh-agent** is a small program running in the background that keeps unlocked keys in memory and answers servers' challenges on ssh's behalf. You type the passphrase once.

Most desktops already run an agent (macOS launchd, GNOME Keyring, Windows' OpenSSH Authentication Agent service). Check with `ssh-add -l`: "The agent has no identities" means it's running but empty; "Could not open a connection" means none is running, so start one with `eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"`.

- `ssh-add` adds your default keys, `ssh-add ~/.ssh/work_ed25519` a specific one.
- `ssh-add -t 8h key` keeps it only for eight hours; `ssh-add -D` removes all keys.
- `AddKeysToAgent yes` in `~/.ssh/config` adds a key automatically the first time you use it.
- On macOS, `UseKeychain yes` stores the passphrase in the Keychain.

ssh finds the agent through the `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` environment variable. It holds the path of a **Unix socket**: a special file that programs on the same machine use to talk to each other. If ssh keeps asking for the passphrase, that variable is usually missing or out of date (common inside tmux or after `sudo`).

Anyone who can reach your agent's Unix socket can use your keys while they are loaded. That's why **agent forwarding** (`ssh -A`), which lets a server you log in to use your agent, is risky on servers you don't fully trust; the jump hosts lesson shows the safer alternative.
concepts.code:
ssh-add -l                     # list loaded keys (or: no identities)
eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"         # start an agent if none is running
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519      # asks for the passphrase once
ssh-add -t 8h ~/.ssh/work_ed25519
echo "$SSH_AUTH_SOCK"          # /tmp/ssh-XXXX/agent.1234
ssh-add -D                     # forget all keys

# ~/.ssh/config
# Host *
#   AddKeysToAgent yes
#   UseKeychain yes            # macOS only
takeaways: The agent holds unlocked keys so you enter the passphrase once
ssh-add -l / ssh-add key / ssh-add -D
SSH_AUTH_SOCK tells ssh where the agent is
pitfalls: Running eval $(ssh-agent) in every shell, starting dozens of agents; reuse the desktop's agent.

quiz.q: ssh keeps asking for your key's passphrase even though you ran ssh-add earlier in another terminal. Most likely?
options: This shell's SSH_AUTH_SOCK points to a different or no agent
ssh-add only works once per boot
quiz.explain: Each shell finds the agent through SSH_AUTH_SOCK; if it is unset or points elsewhere, the loaded key is not visible.

concepts.name: ~/.ssh/config: hosts and aliases
concepts.summary: Describe hosts once in ~/.ssh/config with Host blocks so ssh web just works with the right user, port and key.
concepts.why: A good config file replaces long commands and is used by every SSH-based tool, from scp to Git to VS Code.
concepts.body:
`~/.ssh/config` stores per-host settings. A **Host** line starts a block that applies to matching host names (patterns with `*` and `?` work):

- `HostName` is the real name or IP address; the `Host` name becomes a short nickname for it.
- `User`, `Port`, `IdentityFile` set the login name, port and key.
- `IdentitiesOnly yes` offers only the listed key, avoiding "Too many authentication failures" when the agent holds many keys.
- `ServerAliveInterval 60` sends a tiny "still here" message every 60 seconds, so network equipment along the way doesn't cut an idle connection.

The crucial rule: for each option, **the first value found wins**. ssh reads the file top to bottom and keeps the first match, so put specific `Host` blocks first and general defaults (`Host *`) at the end. Command-line `-o` options beat everything in the file.

Every tool that uses OpenSSH honours this file: `scp web:file .`, `rsync`, `git clone git@github-work:org/repo.git` and code editors' remote features all use the nickname.

To see what ssh will actually use for a host, run `ssh -G web`; it prints the fully resolved configuration. `Include ~/.ssh/config.d/*` lets you split a large config into files (put it near the top).
concepts.code:
# ~/.ssh/config
Host web
    HostName 203.0.113.10
    User deploy
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/work_ed25519
    IdentitiesOnly yes

Host github-work
    HostName github.com
    User git
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/work_ed25519

Host *
    ServerAliveInterval 60
    AddKeysToAgent yes

# usage:  ssh web     scp app.tgz web:/tmp/     git clone git@github-work:acme/api.git
# check:  ssh -G web | grep -E '^(user|hostname|port) '
takeaways: Host blocks define aliases with HostName, User, Port, IdentityFile
First obtained value wins: specific blocks first, Host * last
ssh -G host prints the effective settings
pitfalls: Putting Host * with a User at the top; its User then wins over every later block's User.

quiz.q: Your config has `Host *` with `User root` at the top and `Host web` with `User deploy` below. Which user does `ssh web` use?
quiz.explain: For each option the first obtained value is used, and Host * matched first.

quiz.q: Which command shows the configuration ssh will really use for a host?
quiz.explain: -G prints the resolved configuration after applying all Host and Match blocks, then exits.

concepts.name: scp, sftp and rsync over SSH
concepts.summary: Copy files with scp, browse interactively with sftp, and sync directories efficiently with rsync over SSH.
concepts.why: Moving builds, logs and backups between machines is a constant task, and the right tool saves time and network traffic.
concepts.body:
Three tools copy files over SSH, and all of them use your `~/.ssh/config` aliases and keys.

**scp** copies like `cp`, with `host:path` for remote locations: `scp app.tgz web:/tmp/`, `scp web:/var/log/app.log .`, `-r` for directories, `-P` (capital) for the port. Since OpenSSH 9.0, scp uses the SFTP protocol underneath, which fixed old quoting and security problems with remote paths.

**sftp** is an interactive file session (`ls`, `cd`, `get`, `put`, `lcd` for the local side) and can be scripted with `-b batchfile`. It's also what many point-and-click file-transfer apps use.

**rsync** (a separate program, which must be installed on both ends) is the best choice for directories and repeated copies: it transfers only the differences, can resume, and preserves permissions and times with `-a`.

- `rsync -avz src/ web:/srv/app/` syncs the **contents** of `src` into `/srv/app`.
- Without the trailing slash, `src` itself is created inside the target. This trailing-slash rule is the classic rsync gotcha.
- `--delete` removes files on the target that no longer exist in the source; preview with `-n` (dry run) first.
- `-e 'ssh -p 2222'` passes ssh options.

For a quick one-off file, scp is fine; for anything recurring or large, use rsync.
concepts.code:
scp app.tgz web:/tmp/                  # local -> remote
scp web:/var/log/app.log ./logs/       # remote -> local
scp -r -P 2222 dist/ deploy@host:/srv/ # directory, custom port

sftp web
# sftp> get /var/log/app.log
# sftp> put build.zip /tmp/

rsync -avz --delete -n dist/ web:/srv/app/   # dry run: what would change
rsync -avz --delete dist/ web:/srv/app/      # sync contents of dist/
rsync -avz -e 'ssh -p 2222' data/ backup:/data/
takeaways: scp for quick copies, sftp for interactive sessions, rsync for directories
rsync src/ copies contents; rsync src copies the directory itself
Dry-run rsync --delete with -n before running it for real
pitfalls: Running rsync --delete with the wrong trailing slash or target; always dry-run first.

quiz.q: What is the difference between `rsync -a src web:/dst/` and `rsync -a src/ web:/dst/`?
options: The second only copies new files
The first creates /dst/src, the second copies src's contents into /dst
quiz.explain: A trailing slash on the source means 'the contents of', otherwise the directory itself is copied.

concepts.name: Local port forwarding (-L)
concepts.summary: ssh -L 5433:localhost:5432 db makes a remote service, such as a database, appear on a port of your own machine.
concepts.why: Tunnels let you reach databases and admin web pages that are deliberately not exposed to the internet.
concepts.body:
Some services, like a database, listen only on the server itself, so nobody on the internet can reach them. **Local forwarding** (a kind of **port forwarding**, often called a tunnel) gets you in anyway. ssh opens a port on your machine and carries every connection made to it, through the SSH connection, to a destination as seen **from the server**.

Every machine calls itself `localhost`, so whose `localhost` is meant depends on where you stand. The form is `-L [bind_address:]local_port:destination:destination_port`:

- `ssh -L 5433:localhost:5432 db` forwards your port 5433 to port 5432 on the `db` server itself (`localhost` is looked up on the server side). Now `psql -h localhost -p 5433` talks to the remote PostgreSQL database.
- `ssh -L 8080:internal-api:80 bastion` reaches `internal-api`, a machine that only `bastion` can see. A **bastion** is a server set up as the one way in to private machines you can't reach directly.

Useful companions:

- `-N` runs no remote command (just the tunnel), `-f` goes to the background after logging in.
- `ExitOnForwardFailure yes` makes ssh exit if it can't open the local port, instead of connecting without a tunnel.
- The local port listens on `localhost` only, so only your machine can use it; binding to `0.0.0.0` (all your machine's addresses) would expose it to your network.

Forwards can live in `~/.ssh/config` as `LocalForward 5433 localhost:5432`. Traffic is encrypted between you and the SSH server; from there to the destination it travels unencrypted, so a destination on the server itself (`localhost`) is the safest pattern.
concepts.code:
# expose the remote PostgreSQL on local port 5433
ssh -N -L 5433:localhost:5432 deploy@db.example.com
psql -h localhost -p 5433 -U app shop      # in another terminal

# reach a service only visible from the bastion, in the background
ssh -f -N -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes -L 8080:grafana.internal:3000 bastion
curl -s localhost:8080/api/health

# ~/.ssh/config
# Host db-tunnel
#     HostName db.example.com
#     LocalForward 5433 localhost:5432
takeaways: -L local_port:dest:dest_port, with dest resolved on the server
-N for tunnel only, -f to background, ExitOnForwardFailure for safety
Listeners bind to localhost unless you say otherwise
pitfalls: Reading 'localhost' in -L as your own machine; it is relative to the SSH server.

quiz.q: In `ssh -L 9000:localhost:80 web`, which machine does `localhost` refer to?
quiz.explain: The destination host is resolved and connected to from the SSH server's side.

concepts.name: Bastions and ProxyJump
concepts.summary: Reach private machines through a bastion host with ssh -J or ProxyJump, without copying keys to the bastion or forwarding your agent.
concepts.why: Production networks usually hide servers behind a bastion; ProxyJump is the safe, simple way through.
concepts.body:
Many networks expose only one carefully locked-down **bastion**, also called a **jump host**. Internal servers accept SSH only from it.

`ssh -J bastion app1` connects to the bastion, asks it to open a plain network connection to `app1:22`, and runs a second, end-to-end encrypted SSH session to `app1` **through** that connection. Authentication to `app1` happens from your machine, with your local keys and agent. The bastion only relays encrypted bytes; it never sees your private key or the inner session's contents.

In `~/.ssh/config`:

`Host app* db*` / `ProxyJump bastion` makes `ssh app1` transparent, and every tool (scp, rsync, Git, code editors' remote features) picks it up. Several hops chain with commas: `-J hop1,hop2`.

Compare with the old approach: log in to the bastion with **agent forwarding** (`ssh -A`) and ssh onward from there. That lets anyone with root on the bastion use your agent to authenticate as you to other servers for as long as you are connected. Prefer ProxyJump; if you must forward an agent, do it only to hosts you trust, and consider `ssh-add -c` so each use requires confirmation.

ProxyJump needs forwarding allowed on the bastion (`AllowTcpForwarding`); `ProxyCommand` remains for unusual cases, such as a cloud provider's own tunnel command.
concepts.code:
ssh -J alice@bastion.example.com alice@10.0.3.21     # one-off

# ~/.ssh/config
Host bastion
    HostName bastion.example.com
    User alice
Host app-* db-*
    ProxyJump bastion
    User alice
Host app-1
    HostName 10.0.3.21

# then simply:
#   ssh app-1
#   rsync -av build/ app-1:/srv/app/
takeaways: ssh -J / ProxyJump hops through a bastion end-to-end
The bastion relays encrypted traffic and never holds your keys
Prefer ProxyJump over agent forwarding (-A)
pitfalls: Using ssh -A to every bastion; a compromised bastion can then use your agent.

quiz.q: Why is ProxyJump safer than logging into the bastion with -A and then sshing onward?
options: Your agent is never exposed to the bastion; authentication to the target happens from your machine
quiz.explain: With -A, the bastion can ask your agent to sign; with ProxyJump it only forwards encrypted bytes.

concepts.name: Remote (-R) and dynamic (-D) forwarding
concepts.summary: -R exposes a port of your machine on the server, and -D turns ssh into a SOCKS proxy, a relay that reaches any destination.
concepts.why: Reverse tunnels and SOCKS proxies solve 'show my local app to a remote machine' and 'browse as if I were inside that network'.
concepts.body:
**Remote forwarding** is the mirror of `-L`: the **server** listens and forwards connections back to a destination as seen from **your** machine.

`ssh -R 8080:localhost:3000 demo` makes port 8080 on `demo` reach the app you're developing on your laptop's port 3000. By default that port listens on the server's `localhost` only; making it reachable from other machines needs `GatewayPorts yes` (or `clientspecified`) in the server's sshd_config. Remote forwarding is also how a machine that can't accept incoming connections (say, on a home internet connection) can "phone home" and be reached; `autossh` or a systemd service keeps such a tunnel running.

**Dynamic forwarding** `-D 1080` starts a local **SOCKS proxy**: a relay that apps can ask to connect them to any address. Each connection an application makes through it is forwarded to whatever destination it asks for, resolved and connected from the server. Point a browser or `curl --socks5-hostname localhost:1080` at it to reach internal dashboards as if you were on the server's network. `--socks5-hostname` (rather than `--socks5`) makes the server look up names (DNS), which internal names need.

Both appear in `~/.ssh/config` as `RemoteForward` and `DynamicForward`. Server admins control these features with `AllowTcpForwarding` (and `PermitListen` / `PermitOpen` for fine-grained limits).
concepts.code:
# share your local app (port 3000) as port 8080 on the server's loopback
ssh -N -R 8080:localhost:3000 demo.example.com
#   on demo:  curl localhost:8080   -> served by your laptop

# SOCKS proxy through the bastion
ssh -N -D 1080 bastion
curl --socks5-hostname localhost:1080 http://grafana.internal:3000/api/health

# ~/.ssh/config
# Host bastion-proxy
#     HostName bastion.example.com
#     DynamicForward 1080
takeaways: -R remote_port:dest:port listens on the server, forwards to your side
-D port runs a SOCKS5 proxy; use remote DNS resolution
GatewayPorts and AllowTcpForwarding control these on the server
pitfalls: Expecting -R ports to be reachable from outside the server without GatewayPorts.

quiz.q: You run `ssh -D 1080 bastion` and want curl to resolve internal hostnames on the bastion side. Which option?
quiz.explain: --socks5-hostname sends the hostname to the proxy, so resolution happens remotely.

concepts.name: Configuring and hardening sshd
concepts.summary: Lock down an SSH server: keys only, no root password logins, limited users, and safe config testing before reload.
concepts.why: Internet-facing SSH servers are attacked constantly; a few sshd_config lines remove most of the risk.
concepts.body:
The server reads `/etc/ssh/sshd_config`. Many distributions include `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf` at the top of it, and like the client, sshd uses **the first value it finds** for each setting, so a small extra file in that folder (a **drop-in**) wins over later lines in the main file.

A sensible baseline once your key login works:

- `PasswordAuthentication no` and `KbdInteractiveAuthentication no`: keys only, which defeats password-guessing bots.
- `PermitRootLogin no` (the default is `prohibit-password`, which still allows root with a key). Log in as a user and use sudo.
- `AllowUsers deploy alice` or `AllowGroups ssh-users` to restrict who can log in at all.
- `AuthenticationMethods publickey` to be explicit; `MaxAuthTries 3` to limit guesses per connection.
- `X11Forwarding no` (showing remote graphical windows on your screen), and `AllowTcpForwarding no` on hosts that do not need tunnels.

**Apply changes safely.** Run `sudo sshd -t` to check for mistakes, keep your current session open, reload (`systemctl reload ssh` on Debian/Ubuntu, `sshd` on RHEL/Fedora), and test a **new** login from another terminal before closing the old one. Locking yourself out of a remote server is the classic mistake.

`Match` blocks apply settings conditionally: `Match User backup` followed by `ForceCommand /usr/local/bin/backup-receiver` restricts one account. `sshd -T` prints the effective configuration. Tools that block addresses after repeated failed logins (fail2ban, firewall rules) help, but don't replace key-only login.
concepts.code:
# /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/10-hardening.conf
PasswordAuthentication no
KbdInteractiveAuthentication no
PermitRootLogin no
AllowGroups ssh-users
MaxAuthTries 3
X11Forwarding no

Match User backup
    ForceCommand /usr/local/bin/backup-receiver
    AllowTcpForwarding no

# apply safely (keep your current session open!)
# sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl reload ssh
# sudo sshd -T | grep -i passwordauthentication
takeaways: Keys only: PasswordAuthentication no, KbdInteractiveAuthentication no
PermitRootLogin no and AllowUsers/AllowGroups limit who gets in
sshd -t, reload, test a new login before closing the old session
pitfalls: Disabling passwords before confirming key login works for your account, then losing access.

quiz.q: You disabled password authentication and reloaded sshd. What should you do before closing your current session?
options: Open a new terminal and confirm you can still log in
quiz.explain: Existing sessions survive a reload; a fresh login proves the new config does not lock you out.

concepts.name: Connection multiplexing (ControlMaster)
concepts.summary: Reuse one authenticated SSH connection for many sessions with ControlMaster, ControlPath and ControlPersist.
concepts.why: Multiplexing makes repeated ssh, scp, rsync and Ansible calls near-instant and reduces load on bastions.
concepts.body:
Every new SSH connection pays for setup: connecting, agreeing on encryption keys and logging in, often hundreds of milliseconds, more through a bastion, plus a hardware-key touch if you use one. **Multiplexing** lets later sessions ride on an existing connection as extra **channels**: separate streams of traffic sharing one connection.

Three options:

- `ControlMaster auto`: the first connection becomes the master and opens a Unix socket for later ones; later ones use it if present.
- `ControlPath ~/.ssh/cm-%C`: where that Unix socket lives. `%C` is a hash of host, port, user and jump settings, keeping paths short and unique (Unix socket paths are limited to about 100 bytes).
- `ControlPersist 10m`: keep the master open in the background for ten minutes after the last session closes.

Control the master with `-O`: `ssh -O check web` shows whether it is running, `ssh -O exit web` closes it, `ssh -O forward -L 5433:localhost:5432 web` adds a port forward to an existing connection.

Trade-offs to know: all sessions share one network connection, so a stalled network stalls them all; connection-level options given to later commands (ciphers, compression, keepalives) are ignored because the master's settings apply; and if the server revokes your key, an open master still works until it closes. Ansible enables multiplexing by default for exactly the speed reason.
concepts.code:
# ~/.ssh/config
Host *
    ControlMaster auto
    ControlPath ~/.ssh/cm-%C
    ControlPersist 10m

# first connection authenticates and becomes the master
ssh web 'true'
time ssh web 'true'          # real 0m0.05s instead of ~0.5s
ssh -O check web             # Master running (pid=4242)
ssh -O forward -L 5433:localhost:5432 web   # add a tunnel to it
ssh -O exit web              # Exit request sent.
takeaways: ControlMaster auto + ControlPath + ControlPersist = reuse connections
%C in ControlPath gives a short unique Unix socket name
ssh -O check/exit/forward manages the master
pitfalls: Changing options for a host while a master is running and seeing no effect; ssh -O exit first.

quiz.q: Three sessions share one ControlMaster connection and the network path stalls. What happens?
options: All three stall, because they share one network connection
The master moves to another socket
quiz.explain: Multiplexed sessions are channels on a single connection, so they share its fate.

concepts.name: SSH certificates and CAs
concepts.summary: Sign user and host keys with an SSH certificate authority so servers trust a CA instead of individual keys, with expiry built in.
concepts.why: At scale, certificates replace sprawling authorized_keys and known_hosts files with short-lived, centrally issued credentials.
concepts.body:
Managing `authorized_keys` on hundreds of servers, and `known_hosts` on every laptop, does not scale. OpenSSH supports its own **certificates** (not the kind websites use): a public key plus details such as who owns it, which logins it allows and until when, all signed by a **certificate authority (CA)**. In SSH a CA is simply a key pair that every server and laptop agrees to trust.

**User certificates.** The CA signs a user's public key with an identity, a list of **principals** (allowed login names) and a validity period:

`ssh-keygen -s user_ca -I alice@corp -n alice,deploy -V +8h id_ed25519.pub` produces `id_ed25519-cert.pub`, which ssh picks up automatically next to the key. Servers need just one line, `TrustedUserCAKeys /etc/ssh/user_ca.pub`, and accept any valid certificate whose principals include the target account. Short validity (hours) means you rarely need revocation; `RevokedKeys` handles the rest.

**Host certificates.** Sign each server's host key with `-h`: `ssh-keygen -s host_ca -h -I web1 -n web1.example.com ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub`, configure `HostCertificate` in sshd, and clients trust all of them with one known_hosts line: `@cert-authority *.example.com ssh-ed25519 AAAA...`. No more first-connect prompts or changed-key warnings after rebuilds.

`ssh-keygen -L -f id_ed25519-cert.pub` shows a certificate's contents. Tools like Vault, step-ca and Teleport hand out certificates automatically after a company-wide login (single sign-on).
concepts.code:
# CA side: create CAs once, keep them very safe
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f user_ca -C "user CA"
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f host_ca -C "host CA"

# issue an 8-hour certificate for alice, valid for logins as alice or deploy
ssh-keygen -s user_ca -I alice@corp -n alice,deploy -V +8h ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
ssh-keygen -L -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519-cert.pub     # inspect principals and validity

# server: /etc/ssh/sshd_config
#   TrustedUserCAKeys /etc/ssh/user_ca.pub
#   HostCertificate /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key-cert.pub
# sign the host key:
ssh-keygen -s host_ca -h -I web1 -n web1.example.com /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub
# client: ~/.ssh/known_hosts
#   @cert-authority *.example.com ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3Nz... host CA
takeaways: A CA signs user keys (principals + validity) and host keys (-h)
Servers: TrustedUserCAKeys; clients: @cert-authority in known_hosts
Short-lived certificates make revocation mostly unnecessary
pitfalls: Forgetting -n principals: a certificate with no principals is not accepted for any login by default on servers using TrustedUserCAKeys.

quiz.q: What does a server need in order to accept user certificates from your CA?
options: TrustedUserCAKeys pointing at the CA's public key
Every user's public key in authorized_keys
quiz.explain: The server only needs the CA public key; it then trusts any valid certificate with a matching principal.

concepts.name: How the SSH protocol works
concepts.summary: SSH-2 layers a transport (key exchange, encryption, host auth), user authentication and multiplexed channels on one network connection.
concepts.why: Understanding the layers explains debug output, algorithm errors, forwarding and multiplexing behaviour.
concepts.body:
SSH version 2 (RFC 4251-4254) is built in three layers over one **TCP** connection (the internet's standard reliable connection, which delivers bytes complete and in order).

**Transport layer.** Both sides send a version string, then exchange lists of supported algorithms and pick the first client preference the server also supports: key exchange, host key type, cipher (encryption method) and MAC (a check value that detects tampering). The **key exchange** (Diffie-Hellman style) lets both sides arrive at the same secret keys without ever sending them; the server signs the exchange with its **host key**, which is what your known_hosts check verifies. OpenSSH 10.0 defaults to the hybrid post-quantum `mlkem768x25519-sha256` key exchange, which pairs a new quantum-resistant method with classic X25519 so a future quantum computer cannot decrypt recorded traffic. Ciphers are typically `chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com` or AES-GCM. Keys are periodically re-exchanged (`RekeyLimit`).

**User authentication.** Inside the encrypted transport the client tries methods (`publickey`, `password`, `keyboard-interactive`...). For publickey, the client signs data bound to the session ID, so a signature cannot be replayed on another connection.

**Connection layer.** Everything else is **channels** multiplexed over the connection: an interactive session, a single remote command, an `sftp` subsystem, each forwarded TCP connection (`direct-tcpip` for `-L`, `forwarded-tcpip` for `-R`), agent forwarding. That is why ControlMaster can add sessions cheaply.

`ssh -vvv` shows each step; `ssh -Q kex` (or `cipher`, `key`) lists supported algorithms. Errors like "no matching host key type found" mean the algorithm negotiation found no overlap, typically with very old servers using deprecated algorithms (ssh-rsa with SHA-1, DSA, which 10.0 removed entirely).
concepts.code:
ssh -vvv web 2>&1 | grep -E 'kex: algorithm|host key algorithm|cipher|Authenticat'
# debug1: kex: algorithm: mlkem768x25519-sha256
# debug1: kex: host key algorithm: ssh-ed25519
# debug1: kex: server->client cipher: chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com ...
# debug1: Authenticated to web ([203.0.113.10]:22) using "publickey".
ssh -Q kex | head -3          # key exchange algorithms this client supports
ssh -Q key                    # supported key types
# talking to a legacy device that only offers ssh-rsa (SHA-1):
ssh -o HostKeyAlgorithms=+ssh-rsa -o PubkeyAcceptedAlgorithms=+ssh-rsa old-switch
takeaways: Transport (kex, cipher, host key) -> user auth -> channels
Hybrid post-quantum key exchange is the default in OpenSSH 10
Forwards, sessions and sftp are all channels on one connection
pitfalls: Permanently re-enabling deprecated algorithms globally (Host *) instead of only for the one legacy host.

quiz.q: What is the host key signature during key exchange used for?
options: Proving the server's identity so the client can check known_hosts
quiz.explain: The server signs the exchange hash with its host key, binding the session to the identity in known_hosts.

quiz.q: A port forward with -L appears in the protocol as what?
options: A direct-tcpip channel on the existing connection
A separate TCP connection to port 22
quiz.explain: Each forwarded connection is opened as a direct-tcpip channel multiplexed over the same SSH connection.
